newsitem.title: INDIA: FEATURE-Indian population snowballs with poverty.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Indian population snowballs with poverty.

text.p: When he showed a condom to a young woman in rural India, J.N. Guzder says she did not know what it was.

"When I first told her it could help her plan her family, she didn't believe me. She abused me and said only God could control that," says Guzder, president of the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry's Socio-economic Development Foundation.
"Then finally when she understood, she started crying. She said, 'Why didn't you come seven years earlier? I would have had five children less'."
Population experts say Guzder's story is a familiar one, and the main reason why more than 50,000 Indian babies are born every day.

Fifty years after India won freedom from colonial rule and swore that eradicating poverty would be a top priority, barely four in every 10 Indian women can read -- an alarming statistic that experts say holds the key to the population puzzle.
"Our biggest lacuna is we are illiterate. A woman has no control over her womb," says Health Minister Renuka Chowdhury.

"The inherent problem in family planning is gender bias. It's not as if we are happy multipliers -- the problem is that male participation is ridiculously low because of our social practices and the entire concept of machismo," she said.
India, the world's second most populous country with 936 million people, supports about 16 percent of the world's population on less than 2.5 percent of its area.
Demographers say it is on course to knock China out of the number one slot by 2050 if current population growth trends continue.
They say part of the problem is that India has focused for decades on sterilisation -- initially for men and then, for women -- as the mainstay of population control.

Of the 41 percent of Indian women who use contraceptives, two thirds resort to sterilisation and a quarter have never heard of the pill, intra-uterine devices (IUDs) or condoms. One in 12 Indian women has her first child before the age of 19.
THE FIRST FAMILY PLANNING PROGRAMME IN THE WORLD
Ironically, India was the first country in the world to officially institute a family planning programme in 1951.
It adopted a much-criticised scheme of setting targets for condom distribution and sterilisations, which included a disastrous attempt at coercive male sterilisation in the 1970s.

Recently, the government decided to drop the target-oriented approach and aggressively push contraceptives. Although buses often parade messages urging people to have just one child, India does not enforce a one-child norm as China does.

"It is fashionable to object to disincentives to having children. It is called an invasion of human rights," says public health expert Karan Singh, who as health minister in 1976 began drafting a national population policy which he says is still in mothballs.
"We also have some sort of moral objections to incentives. And we also say we now want no targets. The result is you end up with no family planning," he said.
When India won independence in 1947, it was home to 340 million people. Today, an equal number live in absolute poverty.
"In population, our performance is nothing short of calamitous," Singh said. "Poverty is a direct function of overpopulation, yet we do not have a sense of urgency about it."
HIGH INFANT MORTALITY SPURS DESIRE FOR CHILDREN
While the average number of children borne by a woman fell to 3.5 in 1993 from six in 1950, infant mortality rates in large parts of poor, rural northern India remained alarmingly high.
Frightened by infant deaths, women typically give birth to several children, reckoning that an extra mouth to feed is more than offset by an additional pair of working hands.
Others keep having babies until they produce male children, traditionally favoured because of social biases against girls.

Population Foundation of India executive director K. Srinivasan says India's population will swell to 1.26 billion over the next 20 years, as the number of women in the child-bearing phase rises to 334 million from 222 million.
With economic development, the death rate has fallen to nine per 1,000 people in 1995 from about 23 in 1951. But the birth rate has remained high, falling to just 28 from 42 per 1,000.
Singh said: "Our family planning programme has fallen into disrepair. Where are we going to produce the jobs, clothing, shelter, food, health and education from?"
"It is possible that Malthusian checks will come into play," he said, referring to an economic theory that says rapid population growth will be checked by food shortages.
"We see that in African countries where population growth is exponential, a third of the population has been wiped out by AIDS. Do not forget that we are sitting on that volcano, too."
